conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the neurology team doctors. You're here today for your sixth cycle of high-dose methotrexate, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been doing okay since the last one, just the floaters again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The visual floaters? You mentioned they usually improve for a few weeks after treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They come back, but they’re not as bad as before. I just hope this round helps again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. We’ll monitor that. Today, you’ll get the methotrexate infusion, and we’ll also do a lumbar puncture to check your CSF.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The spinal tap? Is that necessary every time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because we’re treating lymphoma in the central nervous system. It helps us make sure there’s no active disease in the fluid around your brain and spine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I trust you. Any side effects I should watch for today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some people feel nausea. We’ll give you ondansetron to prevent that. We also monitor your kidneys closely because methotrexate can affect them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My kidneys? I remember last time they were watching that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. We’ll keep you well-hydrated and check your urine pH to protect your kidneys. No citrus or carbonated drinks, okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No problem. I brought water and the diet instructions from last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You just finished the methotrexate infusion. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little queasy, but not bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you some ondansetron to help. Also, your spinal tap went well. The CSF looked clear—no infection or cancer cells seen so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So no signs of the lymphoma spreading?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs today. The cell count was very low, which is good. We’ll get full culture results in a few days, but early looks are reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs show your creatinine is rising a bit—from 0.9 to 1.8. It’s likely due to the methotrexate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? My kidneys were okay before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re seeing early kidney stress, called acute tubular necrosis. But you’re making good urine, so it’s mild. We’ll keep pushing fluids and monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it get worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t expect so. Your urine output is strong, and we’re alkalinizing it. Most patients recover fully with this approach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll keep drinking as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your brain MRI came back. The lesion in your left frontal lobe is unchanged—still consistent with old scarring, or gliosis. No new tumors or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no progression?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: None. That’s excellent news. The treatment seems to be keeping the lymphoma under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a huge relief. What about my eyes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling ocular radiation. It’s a preventive step since you’ve had vitreous involvement before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Radiation to the eyes? Will I lose vision?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Low-dose, targeted treatment. The goal is to prevent lymphoma there. Risk to vision is very low, and we’ll work with radiation oncology to minimize any risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do whatever it takes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is still declining—creatinine is now 2.9. But you’re making urine, so we’re not worried about dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s going up. Should I be concerned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s expected with high-dose methotrexate. We’ve seen this before. As long as you keep making urine, it should recover over the next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the CT of my kidneys? I saw it was done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, showed no stones or blockages. There’s a cyst in your left kidney, but it’s unchanged and not causing the issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. Anything else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes are a bit elevated—ALT and AST are up. But that’s common with methotrexate and should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your methotrexate level at 96 hours is 0.11—very good. That means your body cleared it well. We’re stopping leucovorin now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Leucovorin protects your healthy cells from methotrexate. Once the drug is cleared, we stop it. Your level is low enough that you’re safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. So my kidneys will start getting better now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we expect gradual improvement. Your creatinine will likely stay high for a few more days, but it should trend down at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had a bowel movement? That’s good. We added lactulose because you were constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, finally. The stool softeners help. Is that from the meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Chemo and reduced activity can slow your bowels. We’ll send you home with docusate and senna to keep things moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news: you’re being discharged today. Your condition is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take aspirin daily again, plus docusate twice a day, and senna as needed. Ondansetron and prochlorperazine for nausea if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the kidney? When do I check that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your oncology team will order labs in a few days. Call if you notice less urine, swelling, or feel very unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the eye radiation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get a call to schedule that. It’s important for preventing lymphoma in the eyes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll watch for fevers or breathing issues too, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Go to the ER if you have chest pain, trouble breathing, or a fever over 100.4.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel confident going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. We’ll see you in follow-up. Take care, Mr. Thompson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, just a little tired. But I feel okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. Rest at home. Your body’s recovering from chemo and kidney stress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will review your discharge meds and instructions. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our team is here for you. Call with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final note: your CSF culture came back negative—no growth. That’s excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No infection. That’s one less thing to worry about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your nervous system is stable. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels home. We’ll see you soon for follow-up.
